text: Never pass large data payloads through shell variable expansion or command-line arguments; write to temporary files first and read from them to avoid "Argument list too long" errors.
When investigating unfamiliar codebases, read source files and understand existing code structure before attempting fixes, rather than relying solely on project setup or scaffolding commands.
Always document file paths, database schemas, and error resolutions with concrete details so they can be referenced later; never leave key technical context as vague summaries
When a user explicitly says to skip something (e.g., "ignore unit tests"), immediately comply and remove any related artifacts rather than continuing to generate or propose them.
When a user dislikes a code pattern, immediately propose concrete cleaner alternatives (wrapper functions, decorators, helpers) rather than defending the existing approach.
After gathering research from multiple sources, categorize and prioritize findings explicitly — distinguish critical items from nice-to-haves before presenting recommendations.
When debugging test failures, always include the full error message, exact file path, and line number so the root cause can be located immediately.
When tracing code paths across multiple files, reference specific file paths and line numbers and show how functions connect to each other through the call chain.
When documenting bugs, include a table mapping each file, line number, specific problem, and downstream impact to make the root cause chain explicitly visible.
Structure code exploration results into clearly labeled sections (e.g., location, imports, usage sites, key insights) so findings are immediately actionable for the next implementation step.
When multiple testing strategies are viable, present options to the user for decision rather than repeatedly revising the approach. Decide once, execute once.
Before ending a session with uncommitted or uncertain work, either complete and verify it or explicitly mark it as WIP. Never commit incomplete work across session boundaries.
After reverting a change to a file, document WHY it was reverted. Do not re-attempt the same change without a different, validated approach.
Before benchmarking or debugging performance of any operation, trace its dependency graph to identify all external API calls, and verify those endpoints are healthy first.

For content-heavy files (presentations, docs), draft the full content in conversation first. Only write to the file once the structure and content are finalized — avoid using the file as a scratchpad.
When writing example-driven content, select and finalize all examples before writing them into the file. Do not iterate on example choice inside the file.
For batch creation of similar content files (slides, docs, configs), establish the working approach on the first file, then apply it consistently to all remaining files.
Before undoing changes, decide the exact end state you want and execute it in one step. Plan the undo strategy before starting — don't chain exploratory git operations.
When the same type of edit applies to many files, define the transformation once and apply uniformly. If edits keep failing, the transformation definition is wrong — fix that, not the files.
After 2 consecutive errors on the same operation, stop and diagnose (check paths, permissions, disk space) before retrying. Never retry blindly a third time.

For large content generation tasks (5+ files), always produce a structured outline and get explicit user approval before generating any content. The cost of a planning step is far less than reverting hours of work.
When stuck in a retry loop (>2 attempts), stop completely. Re-evaluate whether the current approach is viable before trying again. Consider an entirely different strategy.
Never pass binary or encoded data through text-based processing pipelines; validate that input chunks contain readable text content before attempting extraction or analysis.
Don't build tooling to observe a known failure — fix or work around the failure itself. New scripts should solve problems, not just report them.
After applying any code change, verify the change is in place before running tests. Read the modified file back to confirm — never assume an edit succeeded.
For files with complex patterns (enums, DSLs, generated structures), read the entire file and understand the pattern before making any edits. Plan all changes as one atomic edit.
For scripts with multiple integration points (shell commands, browser automation, file I/O), write a complete design with all steps before coding. One-pass implementation beats iterative rewriting.
For structured files like ICS/vCal, gather all content changes needed, then make a single comprehensive edit rather than iterative patches.
When making similar edits across multiple files, perfect the pattern on one file first, then apply the validated pattern to remaining files in a single pass.
When a long-running process is confirmed working, don't monitor it in a tight loop. Calculate expected completion time, set one check, and move on to other work.
When bulk operations fail due to an already-identified external dependency issue, stop observing logs and either fix the dependency, mock it, or abort the operation.
For slides with complex layouts (grids, diagrams), describe the visual structure and content outline first, get approval, then implement the markup.
Always validate variables for `undefined`/`null` before applying type coercion operators (like unary `+`), since `+undefined` silently produces `NaN` rather than throwing an error.
When rebuilding Docker services from private registries, authenticate with the registry first using the correct AWS profile before running `--build`, to avoid wasted time on 403 errors.
Validate all type-coerced parameters (e.g., `+value`, `parseInt`) with explicit undefined/null checks before passing them to downstream services or queries.
When rebuilding Docker services from private registries, always rebuild the container image properly instead of copying files directly into the running container as a temporary fix.
Always verify that output contains actionable, human-readable information (file paths, error descriptions, numbered steps) rather than raw encoded or binary data before presenting results.
Always read the actual source code of every function in the call chain before diagnosing a bug — never reason from descriptions or assumptions alone.
When repeated validation errors reference the same enum mismatch pattern, fix the transformation at the mapping layer rather than correcting individual records.
Document each debugging step with the action taken, the resulting error, and the next hypothesis so the troubleshooting chain remains traceable.
Check `~/.aws/credentials` for available profiles before assuming the default profile has access to private registries.
Document architectural constants (concurrency limits, chunk sizes, inter-chunk delays) with their specific values and purpose alongside the pattern description.
Always decode and inspect JWT tokens to confirm user identity, role, and permissions before debugging authorization-related issues.
Always document multi-step workflows with numbered steps and explicit quality gates; never present raw API calls with inline script parsing as a deliverable.
When describing calculation bug fixes, specify the exact file path, line number, and mathematical reasoning explaining why the current logic is wrong and what the correct operation should be.
When documenting financial or mathematical logic, explicitly state the correct order of operations and warn about common pitfalls (e.g., double-counting) with concrete before/after formulas.
When modifying duplicated logic, identify and list ALL locations where the code exists and flag silent divergence risks before making any changes.
Implement a single upstream deduplication step (content hash + normalized-text key) that runs before any proposal enters the validator, eliminating the repeated-evaluation class of failure entirely.

During multi-step e2e verification, append each check's result (timestamp, action, observed value) to a single `verification.log` file, and produce the summary from that log rather than reconstructing state from memory.
Persist `(session_id, detector, span_hash)` triples and dedupe emissions against that set before writing to the failures log.
Always remove redundant context injection that duplicates functionality handled elsewhere (e.g., drop per-prompt lesson pointers when an automated rules system already injects keyword-matched rules).

Add a pre-write guard that blocks Write/Edit operations targeting `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.claude/settings.json`, and similar global config paths unless the user's most recent message explicitly references that file.
When a scratch/temporary file is edited ≥2 times within a short window, stop and consolidate changes into a single Write call with the finalized content; do not iterate on throwaway files.

Before emitting a rule proposal, run a keyword search over `rules.json` and `rules-shared.json` on the proposed directive's key nouns/verbs; if any existing rule's directive matches, update that rule's reinforcement count instead of proposing new.

When a proposed rule shares the same trigger phrase ("when a user dislikes a pattern") and example as an existing rule, reject as duplicate — examples are a strong duplicate signal even when the wording differs.
Structure change summaries with clear categorical headers (e.g., "Removed:", "Kept:") and bullet points explaining the rationale for each decision.
Never process or respond to binary-encoded or base64 blob content as if it were meaningful code or documentation; flag it as corrupted or irrelevant data and skip to actionable content.
Structure system audits with a clear executive summary listing all discovered systems upfront, followed by per-system details including location, key files, and status.
Add session-scoped dedup by `(failure_type, context_hash)`; cap each unique signature to 1 emission per hour to stop floods of identical false-positives.
Always use keyword-matched, pre-filtered rule injection over manual lesson injection to conserve tokens while maintaining effectiveness tracking.
Persist validator decisions to a keyed store `(hash(rule), hash(existing_rules_subset)) → decision`; on cache hit, skip the LLM call entirely.

Add an abstractness filter to rule validation: reject proposals whose verbs are generic ("document", "ensure", "always consider") without a specific trigger object. Require a concrete noun (file type, tool, error signature) in every rule.
Combine proposal-hash caching with full-corpus retrieval so repeat submissions fail fast and first-time submissions see all existing rules before a verdict.

Rules about "research/exploration output format" must be diffed against eqdlcvnw, ajdxf1n7, hs1vq1ht, and at5v24te before proposal; if concept overlap ≥70%, merge into an existing rule instead of creating a new one.
Never inject content into every prompt that can be run manually on-demand; reserve automatic injection for high-value, keyword-matched guidance to conserve tokens.
Always initialize nested object keys before pushing to arrays to avoid runtime errors when building multi-level data structures.
When diagnosing event-driven system failures, compare working event flows against broken ones to isolate the specific configuration gap (e.g., missing subscription, wrong topic).
Always document multi-step workflows with visual diagrams (e.g., mermaid flowcharts) showing each stage, transition trigger, and terminal states rather than prose-only descriptions.
When comparing similar systems, explicitly state which does the job better and why, using concrete mechanisms (pre-filtering, keyword-matching, direct injection) rather than vague comparisons.
Always replace hardcoded color values (e.g., `backgroundColor: 'white'`) with semantic theme tokens or variables to ensure dark mode compatibility throughout the codebase.
When optimizing N+1 query patterns, verify the replacement batch query produces identical results by comparing output at the same indices before removing the old implementation
Always investigate data ordering differences when refactoring sequential database calls into batch queries, as bulk fetches may return results in a different order than individual calls
Never use Bash array syntax (`arr=(...)`, `${#arr[@]}`) in Alpine/Docker containers that use `sh` instead of `bash`; use individual variables or POSIX-compatible iteration patterns instead.
Never attempt query optimizations based on assumptions about API capabilities; read the actual GraphQL schema and client code to confirm batch/bulk endpoints are available before refactoring.
Never leave `.catch(() => {})` patterns scattered across calling code; instead create a wrapper helper that handles errors internally so callers remain clean
Always trace the full data flow through resolvers, helpers, and database queries before modifying GraphQL endpoints, documenting the chain from schema definition to data transformation.
Always trace mock paths to actual module locations in the project's dependency tree before writing test mocks, verifying the module exists at the exact path Jest will resolve.
Always analyze event payloads to determine the most targeted invalidation scope rather than defaulting to broad cache invalidation like `invalidateAll()`
Before writing any test, explicitly confirm the test scope (unit/integration/e2e) and which code paths must be exercised. Design for the correct scope from the first draft.
Always trace the full data flow through event publishers, subscribers, and handlers to identify configuration gaps before implementing cache invalidation or event-driven features
Always include concrete performance metrics (before/after timings, percentage improvements) when reporting optimization results to quantify the impact of changes like N+1 query elimination.
Always format logging standards with concrete code examples showing each log level (info, warn, error) and include required patterns like "Reason:" prefixes in a copyable code block.
Always categorize discovered events or dependencies by their direct impact (e.g., "directly modifies data" vs "indirectly affects cache") to prioritize which ones require immediate handling.
Document environment-specific workarounds (shell compatibility, argument limits, container constraints) inline with the exact error and fix applied, so future sessions can avoid re-discovering them.
Always read and explore existing query patterns and client interfaces in the codebase before writing new data-fetching logic to avoid duplicating or missing available endpoints.
Document the specific performance problem (e.g., "N sequential HTTP calls") before proposing a solution, so the optimization rationale is clear and verifiable.
Document the full chain of event flow (publisher → topic → subscription → queue → consumer) when analyzing distributed event systems, rather than listing files and dependencies in isolation.
Never assume intermediate lookup results are valid; add defensive null checks after every `.find()`, property access, or chained operation before passing values to downstream functions.
When a container dependency issue is identified, fix it once (rebuild image, update volume, or document as known limitation) before continuing. Never proceed hoping the same error won't recur.
Never inline multi-line scripts with complex quoting into `docker exec`. Use `docker cp` to transfer a script file, then execute it inside the container.
Before parallelizing operations, create a dependency matrix (reads/writes per operation) first. If fields are independent, write the full `Promise.all` implementation in one pass — don't iterate.

Never hardcode JWT tokens in commands — use environment variables or config files. Before running authenticated test requests, verify the token is still valid with a simple health check endpoint first.
When checking logs after an action, use time-bounded queries (`--since`, `--tail N`) to isolate new output. If logs show nothing new after one check, the action produced no log output — move on.
Always verify enum value casing matches the database schema exactly (e.g., PascalCase vs UPPER_CASE) before sending data to APIs or databases, as mismatches cause silent failures or cryptic errors.
Prefer application-level verification (API calls, admin endpoints) over raw database queries — they handle connection strings, auth, and schema automatically.
After applying a fix to a running service, confirm the fix is active by checking server restart timestamps against error timestamps before concluding the issue is resolved.

Never manually edit conflict markers in .ai-memory/session-end-events.jsonl. Git is configured with a jsonl-union merge driver that resolves conflicts automatically by combining both sides, deduplicating by (session_id, ts), and sorting by ts. If conflicts appear after a pull or rebase, it means the driver is not registered in this clone — run ./scripts/setup-merge-drivers.sh once, then redo the merge (or `git checkout --merge HEAD .ai-memory/session-end-events.jsonl`). Never edit the file by hand during a merge.
Hash each rule proposal (normalized lowercase, whitespace-stripped) and short-circuit validation if the hash has been seen in the last 30 days — log the dedup hit so pipeline noise is visible.
Treat repeated same-type failures (≥2) as a signal to halt and re-read the task prompt; do not keep invoking mutating tools when the requested output is plain text.
Always quantify token cost per prompt when evaluating whether a learning/memory subsystem earns its context budget, and flag systems whose overhead exceeds their active content.

After classification, write the session id to `reflections-processed.jsonl` regardless of whether reflections were stored; the "skipped" branch must also persist, otherwise empty/template-only sessions get reprocessed indefinitely.
Backtracking detector must require a `tool_use` of an editing tool in the turn — never trigger on text-only assistant messages.

For `git reset --hard <ref>`, only flag as a failure when (a) `<ref>` is a different branch than current HEAD's upstream, or (b) HEAD has unpushed commits being discarded, or (c) the branch is protected; resetting to your own `origin/<same-branch>` is a benign sync.

Failure detectors must skip context where the matched span is inside a quoted prompt (e.g., text following "You are a rule validator" or "Analyze these failures"). Match on actual tool_use, not prose embedding the phrase.
If the same file set is stashed twice in a session, stop and investigate the source of the churn (postinstall, hook, editor) before stashing a third time.
De-duplicate failures by `tool_use_id` before reporting; one tool call should produce at most one failure entry regardless of how many heuristics it trips.

Backtracking detection MUST extract filenames only from `Edit.file_path`, `Write.file_path`, or `NotebookEdit.notebook_path` fields. Ignore filenames inferred from commit messages, console output, or natural-language text.
Validate extracted filenames before counting: must contain at least one `/` or `.<ext>` and length ≥ 3; reject single tokens like `a`, `in`, `is`, `on` as definitionally invalid paths.
Backtracking detection must read `input.file_path` only — never tokenize `Bash.command`. Reject any candidate containing shell metacharacters (`>`, `<`, `&`, `|`, `;`, `$`) before counting.
Always document the replacement mechanism (command or script) when removing a feature, so users retain manual access if needed.
When debugging, distinguish between the actual error type observed (e.g., `NaN`) and the error type expected from the code path (e.g., `TypeError`) to identify which branch is actually executing.
Always quantify the cost of existing systems (token usage, file reads, execution frequency) before proposing consolidation or removal to justify the change with measurable impact.
Reject proposed rules that broaden an existing rule's scope without adding a concrete new requirement; if the only delta is wording, update the existing rule instead of creating a new one.
Every proposed rule must express exactly one trigger and one action; reject compound rules (`X and also Y`) and reject rules whose justification is a single incident with no reinforcement history.
Always track multi-file refactors with a TodoWrite checklist that marks each step completed, so progress remains visible across agents.

When the same `(detector, matched_span)` pair fires more than twice in a session, escalate to "detector misconfiguration" instead of recording further failures, and quarantine that detector for review.
Never leave inline hardcoded color values in components when implementing theming; always route all color decisions through the theme store and MUI palette.

When defaulting or normalizing a date-only value that becomes a stored timestamp, pin it to UTC noon (T12:00:00.000Z), not midnight — midnight renders as the previous day for users in negative-UTC offsets when the backend truncates dates in UTC.
